questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the primary goal of Module 1: SPOT & SHIFT™?

options.text: To learn how to start a company
To train your brain to stop complaining and start creating

questions.explanation: The module trains your brain to move from complaining to creating solutions. (Page 1, Module Overview)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: According to the module, what do most people do when they see a problem?

options.text: They freeze or say "Someone should fix this"

questions.explanation: Most people freeze or pass responsibility on to someone else. (Section 1: The Real Talk)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which part of the brain reacts first when you see a problem?
questions.explanation: The amygdala, the brain's fear center, reacts first to a perceived problem. (Section 2: What's Happening in Your Brain)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is "problem paralysis"?

options.text: Getting stuck in fear/stress without taking action

questions.explanation: Problem paralysis is getting stuck in fear or stress instead of acting. (Section 2)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Activating your Prefrontal Cortex helps you with...
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex governs decision making and innovation. (Section 2)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The module says every time you shift, you literally...

options.text: Re-wire your brain to think like an innovator

questions.explanation: Shifting rewires your brain toward innovative thinking. (Section 2)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the "SPOT & SHIFT" catchphrase mentioned in the module?
questions.explanation: The catchphrase is "Spot the glitch, flip the switch." (Section 2)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How long is the "Problem Spotting Sprint" activity?
questions.explanation: The Problem Spotting Sprint lasts 2 minutes. (Section 3, Activity 1)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the Problem Spotting Sprint, what should you list?

options.text: 3 things that bug you every day

questions.explanation: You list 3 things that bug you every day. (Section 3)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: According to the module, your daily complaints are actually...
questions.explanation: Daily complaints are treated as clues to innovation. (Section 3)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the first S.U.R.G.E.™ Shift Prompt?

options.text: "How can I make money from this?"
"Name ONE small part of this problem you could possibly own"

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the bus stop example, what was the "micro-ownership" action?

options.text: Start a 3-day bottle collection drive with friends

questions.explanation: The micro-ownership action was a 3-day bottle collection drive with friends. (Section 4, Table)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the parents/music example, what micro-action was suggested?

options.text: Create a short reel explaining why the music inspires you

questions.explanation: The suggested micro-action was creating a short reel explaining the music's value. (Section 4, Table)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship

questions.explanation: The student in the Plastic Bottle Game example was from Pune. (Section 5)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What was the reward in the Plastic Bottle Game?

options.text: 1 reward badge on her class group for every 10 bottles

questions.explanation: 30 students got hooked on the Plastic Bottle Game. (Section 5)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The Mini Challenge asks you to pick one problem from your list and write three things. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The three required parts are the SPOT, the SHIFT, and the First Action — not a budget. (Section 6)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What chemical does shifting trigger in your brain?
questions.explanation: Shifting triggers dopamine, the motivation chemical. (Section 7)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Building your "locus of control" means building...
questions.explanation: Locus of control means building power over your own choices. (Section 7)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the "Shift Code" hack you can say out loud?

options.text: "Let me spot it and shift it"

questions.explanation: The Shift Code is the phrase "Let me spot it and shift it." (Section 8)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The Shift Code is compared to which keyboard shortcut?
questions.explanation: The Shift Code is compared to Ctrl+Alt+Delete, a mental reset. (Section 8)

questions.explanation: The challenge asks you to spot 3 problems. (Section 9)

questions.explanation: The monster is called the Problem Monster. (Workbook, Page 3)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship

questions.explanation: The Module 1 badge is called Certified Spotter. (Workbook, Page 15)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What two symbols are on the Module 1 badge?

options.text: Magnifying glass 🔍 with a lightning bolt

questions.explanation: The badge features a magnifying glass with a lightning bolt. (Workbook, Page 15)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: According to the workbook outcome, what do teens see themselves as at the end of Module 1?
questions.explanation: Teens come away seeing themselves as Solution Seekers in training. (Workbook, Outcome)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which part of the brain is known as the "decision and innovation area"?
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex is the decision and innovation area. (Section 2)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: According to the module, entrepreneurs do NOT wait. They ___ problems early.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurs spot problems early instead of waiting. (Section 1)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The "Solution-seeker state" is entered when you trigger which chemical?
questions.explanation: Dopamine triggers entry into the Solution-seeker state. (Section 7)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What should you do with your shifted action according to the homework?

options.text: Post it in your Mindset Journal or on the app

questions.explanation: You post the shifted action in your Mindset Journal or on the app. (Section 9)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Rohan notices that his school's recycling bins are always empty but the regular trash is overflowing. Using the SPOT & SHIFT method, what would be the BEST "Micro-Ownership" shift?

options.text: "The whole school is lazy. I can't fix this."
"I can own one bin near my classroom and put a 'Recycle Here' sign on it."
"I should complain to the principal about everyone."

questions.explanation: Applies the Shift question from Section 4: own one small, specific piece.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Priya is annoyed that her younger brother keeps taking her pens without asking. Using the SHIFT question, what is her "New Micro-Ownership"?

options.text: Create a "Pen Station" box on her desk with a "Ask before borrowing" note.
Tell her parents to buy more pens.

questions.explanation: Applies the "one small piece you can own" concept from the module.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student spots: "The school library is too loud to study." Which is a properly SHIFTED (smaller, specific, ownable) problem?

options.text: "The librarian is bad at her job."
"The corner table near the window has a group that talks loudly at lunch."

questions.explanation: Follows Page 4 Workbook: "Make it smaller, specific."

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Your friend says: "Social media is so toxic." Using the SPOT & SHIFT mindset, how would you coach them to SHIFT it?

options.text: "Name one small part of that toxicity you could own, like how you react to comments."

questions.explanation: Direct application of the S.U.R.G.E. Shift Prompt.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: If the amygdala is the "alarm system" and the prefrontal cortex is the "pilot," what does SPOT & SHIFT do?

options.text: Turns off the alarm and lets the alarm keep ringing
Acknowledges the alarm but lets the pilot take control

questions.explanation: Conceptual application from Section 2.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student says, "I can't start a business, I'm too young." How does Module 1 directly counter this belief?

options.text: By saying age doesn't matter in business
By showing that entrepreneurs spot and shift small problems immediately, starting with their own world
By giving them money to start
By telling them to wait until college

questions.explanation: References Section 1's debunking of the "I'm too young" myth.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: You spot: "My mom is always stressed about grocery shopping." What is a Level 2 SHIFT action?

options.text: "I can own creating a simple 'Master Grocery List' on the fridge that we check every Sunday."

questions.explanation: Application of "own one piece" from Section 4.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which scenario BEST demonstrates "Problem Paralysis"?

options.text: A student sees a leaky tap and fixes it.
A student sees a leaky tap, feels angry, says "The school never fixes anything," and walks away.
A student sees a leaky tap and tells a friend.
A student sees a leaky tap and starts a plumbing business.

questions.explanation: Direct application of the definition from Section 2.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The Plastic Bottle Game worked because the student shifted from "fix the whole town" to...

options.text: "Own the plastic bottles near her bus stop"

questions.explanation: Direct reference to Section 5's case study.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How would you apply the "Shift Code" (Ctrl+Alt+Delete) during a math test when you feel stuck and frustrated?

options.text: Say "Let me spot it and shift it" to tell your brain to stop freezing and look for one small part you can solve

questions.explanation: Application of the Shift Code from Section 8.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A team project is failing because no one is communicating. What is the SHIFT (ownable piece)?

options.text: "I can own sending a 'Daily 5-Minute Check-in' message to the group"

questions.explanation: Applies Section 4 logic of ownable micro-actions.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The workbook says "Complaints are just solutions in disguise." What does that mean for a student who complains "The school bus is always late"?

options.text: It means they should stop complaining.
It means the solution might be to track the bus timing for one week and suggest a better route.
It means they should buy a car.
It means it's not a real problem.

options.text: Creativity becomes their default mode (new neural pathways)

questions.question: The "Peer Power" activity (Page 10) suggests exchanging frustrations with a friend. Why is this valuable?

Because it's fun to complain together.
Because friends will solve your problems for you.

questions.question: A student shifts "My phone battery dies too fast" to "I can own creating a 'Charge Hour' schedule at 4 PM daily." What is the FIRST ACTION they should take in 24 hours?

questions.explanation: Follows Section 6: "The tiniest step you'll take in 24 hours."

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the difference between "Spot" and "Shift"?

options.text: Spot is for school, Shift is for home.

Spot is complaining; Shift is ignoring.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student says, "I spotted that my class group chat is chaotic." Which Shift option follows the example in Section 6?

"I will start a new group chat."

questions.explanation: Direct example from Section 6.

questions.question: According to Module 1, what happens to your SSI (Solution Seeker Index) when you complete the mini quiz?

questions.explanation: Therapeutic/reframing application. (Workbook, Page 13)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which statement shows a student has successfully built their "locus of control"?

questions.explanation: Definition of locus of control from Section 7.

questions.question: You're the curriculum architect. A Class 8 student shifts "My room is messy" to "I can't clean it all." What would you tell them?

questions.question: How does the "Solution-seeker state" (Section 7) differ from "Problem paralysis" (Section 2)?

options.text: One is for adults, one is for kids.
One is active/creative, the other is frozen/stressed.
One uses the amygdala, the other uses the foot.

questions.question: A student has a "SPOT": There are no dustbins in the playground. Which SHIFT shows the correct "Micro-Ownership"?

options.text: "I will clean the whole playground myself every day."
"I can own requesting one dustbin near the swing set from the school committee."

questions.explanation: Follows the "one small part you could possibly own" rule.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why does the module suggest saying the Shift Code out loud?

questions.explanation: Direct rationale from Section 8.

questions.question: What does "Unbundle & Understand" (the next module) likely refer to?

How to start a company legally

"The WiFi is slow. Someone should fix this."

Never go to the park again

questions.question: The DNA mutation visual (Workbook, Page 12) is used to teach that...

options.text: Each time you shift, you permanently improve your problem-solving ability
You need a lab coat to be an entrepreneur
DNA has nothing to do with mindset

questions.explanation: Metaphor for lasting neural change. (Workbook, Page 12)

questions.question: If a student says, "I spotted 10 problems but I'm overwhelmed," what should you remind them from Module 1?

options.text: "Spotting is enough. You don't need to shift."
"You only need to SHIFT one small part of one problem and start there."

questions.explanation: Sections 4 and 6 emphasize naming one small ownable part.

questions.question: Why is "I'm too young" considered a myth in this module?

options.text: Because age is just a number
Because spotting and shifting problems requires no legal age or permission, only awareness
Because young people have more money

questions.explanation: Section 1 debunks this myth specifically.

questions.question: A student shifts "Parents don't understand my career choice" to "I can create a 5-slide presentation about my career path to show them." This works because it...

options.text: Moves from vague complaint to ownable, proactive communication

questions.explanation: Follows the pattern in Section 4's music example.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student uses SPOT & SHIFT perfectly for 3 weeks. According to neuroplasticity principles in Section 2 & 7, what is the LONG-TERM structural change?

options.text: Their prefrontal cortex develops stronger neural pathways, making solution-seeking automatic

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Evaluate these three responses to "My pocket money is too low." Which one BEST demonstrates the SPOT & SHIFT philosophy AND an entrepreneurial mindset?

"I spotted that my neighbors' dogs need walking. I can own walking 2 dogs for ₹50 each per week."
"I'll wait until I'm 18 to earn money."

questions.subject: entrepreneurship

"I can own a '30-min Peer Mentorship Circle' for 10 juniors every Friday."

questions.explanation: Ownable, specific, immediate — not an attempt to fix the whole system.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Compare the Pune Plastic Bottle Game (Section 5) with a student who says "I'll clean the whole city." Why is the Pune student's approach more effective according to the module?

options.text: Because cleaning the whole city is impossible, but owning a bus stop is achievable and creates momentum (dopamine loop)
Because the Pune student had more friends
Because plastic bottles are easy to clean
Because the whole city is not a real problem

questions.explanation: Evaluates efficacy based on locus of control and dopamine triggers.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student argues: "Shifting small problems doesn't matter because global warming and poverty are the real issues." How would you use Module 1 concepts to respond?

options.text: "SPOT & SHIFT trains your brain to solve problems. The same neural pathways you build fixing the canteen will help you solve climate change later."

questions.explanation: Transfers the skill built from micro problems to macro problems.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: You are designing a new activity for Module 1. Which scenario would BEST teach the difference between "problem-focused thinking" (amygdala) and "solution-focused thinking" (PFC)?

options.text: A role-play where one student says "This is impossible" and another says "What's one thing I can try?"

questions.explanation: Active demonstration of the cognitive shift between brain states.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student successfully shifts "soggy samosas" to "talk to canteen about draining oil." According to the module, what is the SECOND-ORDER effect (the deeper win beyond better samosas)?

options.text: They get free samosas for life
They have wired their brain to see themselves as someone who creates solutions, not victims of problems
The canteen owner becomes their best friend

questions.explanation: Identity shift and neural rewiring — the core goal of the module.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Analyze this: A student SPOTS "The school doesn't have a music club" and SHIFTS to "I will ask permission to start one." They then stop because the principal says "Maybe later." According to the module, what did they forget?

They should have started without permission.

questions.explanation: They missed the iterative action loop emphasized by the module's tiny, consistent actions.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A teacher wants to use the "Shift Code" hack for an entire class that feels stuck on a difficult project. What is the BEST implementation?

Tell them to memorize it silently
Use it as a password for the class computer
Ignore it and give more homework

questions.explanation: Collective verbal anchoring to shift state, per Section 8.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The workbook includes a "Draw your own Problem Monster" activity (Page 3). What psychological purpose does this serve in the SPOT & SHIFT framework?

questions.explanation: Therapeutic externalization makes the monster feel smaller. (Workbook, Page 3)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student has these three frustrations: 1) No parking at school, 2) Too much homework, 3) No healthy snacks. Using the module's prioritization method (what's NOT stated but implied), which should they shift FIRST?

options.text: The one with the smallest, most ownable first action they can take in 24 hours
The one their parents complain about
The one that makes them the angriest

questions.explanation: Inferred from "the tiniest step you'll take in 24 hours" prioritizing momentum first.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How does the "Certified Spotter" badge (Page 15) function as a behavioral reinforcement mechanism?

options.text: It is a final exam grade
It provides external validation and a milestone marker, releasing dopamine and encouraging repetition of the SPOT & SHIFT behavior
It is a license to start a business

questions.explanation: Gamification and positive reinforcement drive repeated behavior. (Workbook, Page 15)

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student argues: "My SHIFT of 'talk to the canteen' failed because they said no." Using the module's growth mindset, what should they do NEXT?

SPOT a NEW problem within the rejection (e.g., "They said no because of budget") and SHIFT again (e.g., "I can find a low-cost healthy option")
Complain to the principal about the canteen
Start a social media war against the canteen

questions.explanation: Iterative application — problems, even rejection, are treated as clues.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The module states: "Every time you repeat this, your brain makes new neural pathways." If a student repeats SPOT & SHIFT 50 times, what cognitive skill has likely developed?

options.text: Automatic problem-framing and solution-seeking as a default response to any frustration

questions.explanation: Definition of habituation and skill automaticity.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Compare two students: Student A shifts "bus stop dirty" by cleaning it once. Student B gamifies it with badges. According to Section 5 & 7, why is Student B's approach SUPERIOR?

questions.question: A student says: "I spotted that my friend is being bullied online. What's my SHIFT?" Which answer BEST aligns with the module's ethical framework (own your piece, don't save the world alone)?

"I can own being the one person who sends my friend one supportive DM every day and encourages them to talk to a teacher."

questions.explanation: Ownable, supportive, within locus of control, escalates appropriately.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The module mentions "locus of control" (Section 7). A student with a strong internal locus of control who fails at a shift would say:

questions.explanation: Internal attribution and adaptive response, per Section 7.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How would you redesign the "Frustration Journal" (Page 6) for a digital native Class 12 student to make it more engaging while keeping the SPOT & SHIFT core?

Create a TikTok-style "Frustration to Fix" 15-second video template where they act out the SPOT and then the SHIFT

questions.explanation: Adapts the medium while preserving the underlying pedagogy. (Workbook, Page 6)

options.text: "I can own forming a 'Study Buddy' system where 3 of us compare notes after class and teach each other the missed steps."

questions.explanation: Collaborative, proactive, blame-free, and creates a peer solution.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The module says "entrepreneurs don't wait." In the context of a Class 8 student, what does "entrepreneur" mean?

options.text: Someone who owns a big factory
Anyone who spots a problem and shifts into action, regardless of age or business registration
Someone with a lot of money
Someone who works in a startup

questions.explanation: Redefines entrepreneur as a mindset rather than a job title.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student perfectly completes the 24-Hour Spot Challenge for 30 days. According to the IDEA DNA model (Workbook, Page 12), what is the state of their "S" nucleotide?

options.text: It is permanently mutated and glowing, meaning problem-spotting is now a reflex

questions.explanation: Long-term habituation and neural mutation, per the workbook's DNA metaphor. (Workbook, Page 12)

questions.question: You have a student who only spots problems but never shifts them. According to Module 1, what is the most likely missing piece in their practice?

questions.explanation: Addresses the root cause of "feeling unheard" with an ownable mechanism.

Wait for someone else to fix it

Getting stuck in a problem without moving to action
Solving too many problems at once

She focused on plastic bottles near her bus stop

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: According to Module 1, entrepreneurs see problems and ________.
questions.explanation: The key mindset: 'Most people see problems and stop. Entrepreneurs see problems and start.'

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does 'micro-ownership' mean in the context of Spot & Shift™?

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The Spot & Shift™ Shift Prompt asks you to name ________ small part of the problem you could own.

questions.question: What is the 'Problem Monster' in the Module 1 Workbook?

A cartoon representing fear and overwhelm from problems

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What do 'Spot & Shift Glasses' represent in the workbook?

questions.explanation: The glasses represent the entrepreneurial lens: wearing them means you see complaints as clues, not dead ends.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is a 'solution-seeker state'?

questions.question: Fred Katz's quote in the workbook says: 'Enterprising minds don't dwell on problems; they look for ______.'

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the 'Frustration Journal' activity in the workbook?

questions.explanation: The Frustration Journal transforms everyday annoyances into entrepreneurial raw material — the first step to spotting real-world problems.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What happens to your brain every time you repeat the Spot & Shift™ process?

questions.explanation: Every time you shift, you literally re-wire your brain — new neural pathways form that make creativity and solution-seeking your natural default mode.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three things stated about why entrepreneurs stand apart?

options.text: They shift into action faster than anyone else
They have more money than everyone
They don't wait for someone else to act

questions.explanation: Speed, awareness and personal initiative define entrepreneurs in this framework — not starting capital or financial advantage.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does the 'Peer Power' activity in the workbook involve?

options.text: Exchanging frustrations with a friend and shifting each other's problems

questions.explanation: Peer Power is about collaborative spotting — sometimes a friend sees an angle in your frustration that you can't see yourself.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: According to Module 1, complaints are raw material for what?
questions.explanation: Complaints are explicitly reframed as clues to innovation — they reveal where things are broken and where entrepreneurs can step in.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the module's 'Mindset Journal'?

options.text: A place to record your Spot, Shift and Action as part of the homework

questions.explanation: The Mindset Journal is where you record your 24-hour challenge — Spot, Shift and tiny action — creating a habit of reflective entrepreneurial thinking.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What are the Spot & Shift™ Cut-Out Cards used for?

options.text: Prompt cards that help you break down any problem you're facing

questions.explanation: The DIY cut-out cards give you portable prompts like 'What's the smallest piece of this problem you can own?' — so you can Spot & Shift anywhere.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student says 'My school canteen food is too oily.' What is the most effective SHIFT for this?

options.text: Talk to the canteen about introducing one healthy dish per week

questions.explanation: The SHIFT focuses on the smallest ownable action — not fixing the whole menu, but introducing one change you can propose directly.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What distinguishes a SPOT from a mere complaint?

options.text: A SPOT is specific, written down and treated as a clue to a solution
A SPOT is about someone else's problem
A SPOT is always about money

questions.explanation: A complaint is passive and emotional. A SPOT is precise, recorded, and treated as raw material — the same problem reframed as data.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why does the Spot & Shift™ framework focus on owning 'one small part' of a problem rather than the whole thing?

options.text: Because big problems can't be solved
Because micro-ownership creates immediate action and avoids overwhelm
Because schools only allow small projects

questions.explanation: Micro-ownership breaks paralysis. You can't change everything, but you can change something — and that one action triggers momentum.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The SURGE Shift Prompt says: 'Name ONE small part of this problem you could possibly ____.'
questions.explanation: 'Own' is the key word — it implies personal responsibility, which is the foundation of entrepreneurial thinking.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How did the Pune student's SHIFT reduce the scale of her problem from 'garbage everywhere' to something actionable?

options.text: She narrowed it to plastic bottles at one specific bus stop
She wrote a petition to the government

questions.explanation: She zoomed in from 'the whole city' to 'plastic bottles + bus stop' — making an impossible problem into a winnable micro-mission.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What psychological concept does regularly practising Spot & Shift™ build in students?
questions.explanation: Locus of control — the belief that your actions influence outcomes — is built every time a student shifts from helplessness to micro-ownership.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: If a student's problem is 'The class group chat is chaotic,' what is a valid SHIFT?

options.text: Design a 'Daily Focus' thread to keep it organised

questions.explanation: The shift creates ownership — designing a system within an existing problem rather than exiting or escalating it.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The module uses the analogy 'Spot the glitch → ________' to describe the SHIFT action.
questions.explanation: 'Spot the glitch → Flip the switch' — a modern tech-era metaphor for moving from problem awareness to solution activation.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which trio of outcomes does Module 1 state you've achieved after completing the Spot & Shift™ process once?

options.text: Locus of control, Dopamine trigger, Solution-seeker state

questions.explanation: Three simultaneous outcomes: you build locus of control (ownership), trigger dopamine (motivation), and enter the solution-seeker state (creative mode).

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the workbook's comic strip, 'Samosa soggy' is shifted to which specific observation?
questions.explanation: The shift makes the problem specific and solvable — 'oil not drained properly' points to a fixable process, unlike the vague 'samosas are bad.'

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why is 'There is garbage everywhere' NOT yet a good SPOT?

options.text: It's too large and vague to act on

questions.explanation: A good SPOT is specific and ownable. 'Garbage everywhere' is a landscape, not a target. 'Plastic bottles at my bus stop' is a SPOT.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the entrepreneurial significance of the Pune student's result — 30 students participating in 3 weeks?

options.text: It proves you need a team
It shows that one person's micro-shift can create community-scale impact
It shows that gamification always works

questions.explanation: One student's micro-ownership spread to 30 participants. This is the startup principle: solve for one, scale to many — it starts with a single shift.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How does the module describe the amygdala's role in problem-solving?

options.text: It helps you focus on solutions
It reacts with fear/stress first, potentially causing you to stay stuck

questions.explanation: The amygdala fires first with stress or anger — if you remain in that state, you get stuck. The SHIFT is what moves you past it to the prefrontal cortex.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the relationship between Spot & Shift™ and SSI™ (Solution-Seeking Index)?

options.text: Each completed SPOT & SHIFT adds points to your SSI score
SSI replaces Spot & Shift in higher classes

questions.explanation: Every time you SPOT, SHIFT, and take action, your SSI score grows — it's a behavioral credential that tracks your capability, not just your knowledge.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does 'mutating your IDEA DNA' mean in the workbook?

options.text: Each Spot & Shift builds a new entrepreneurial thinking pattern in your mind

questions.explanation: 'IDEA DNA' is a metaphor — every S.U.R.G.E.™ module activates a new 'nucleotide' in your entrepreneurial mindset, making innovation instinctive over time.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why does the workbook frame frustrations as 'clues' rather than 'complaints'?

options.text: To make students feel better about failing
To reposition problems as signals pointing to unmet needs and innovation opportunities

questions.explanation: A clue leads somewhere. A complaint doesn't. Reframing frustration as a clue shifts your relationship with problems — from stuck to curious.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'Reflection Page' in the workbook?

options.text: To help students emotionally process what they learned and connect it to their experience

questions.explanation: Reflection is a learning amplifier — 'What felt easiest to shift?' builds metacognition, helping students understand their own thinking process.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student spots: 'Autos block the school gate at 3 PM.' What level of SHIFT would be most appropriate for a Class 9 student?

options.text: Write a letter to the Chief Minister
Create a hand-drawn sign requesting autos to park 10 metres away

questions.explanation: A Class 9-level SHIFT is local, immediate, and personally executable — not bureaucratic or aspirational. A visible sign is micro-ownership.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the 'First Action' element in the Mini Challenge, and why is it important?

options.text: The tiniest concrete step you take within 24 hours — turns intention into momentum

questions.explanation: The 24-hour action window is critical — it prevents 'shift paralysis' where you have the insight but never act. Speed is an entrepreneurial muscle.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: If a student's frustration is 'Science worksheets repeat the same 10 questions,' what SPOT would be most precise?

options.text: Science worksheets use repetitive questions that add no new thinking challenge

questions.explanation: A precise SPOT names the specific mechanism of the problem — not who's to blame, but what's actually happening. Specificity opens the door to a solution.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How does gamification support the entrepreneurial SHIFT, as shown by the Pune student's example?

options.text: It creates an incentive loop that makes participation in a solution feel rewarding
It reduces the quality of work
It only works for younger children

questions.explanation: Gamification (badges, rewards, challenges) taps into the dopamine system — the same motivational chemistry the module describes — to sustain action.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does the 'Spot & Shift™ Table' in the main module document teach students to do?

options.text: Map any problem to a shift question and a specific micro-ownership

questions.explanation: The table trains a three-column thinking habit: Problem → Shift Question → Micro-Ownership. This is the core reasoning template of the module.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the key difference between 'Big Problem' and 'Micro Problem' in the workbook?

options.text: Big problems are real, micro problems are made up
A micro problem is specific enough for one person to act on

questions.explanation: 'Big problem → Micro problem = My problem.' The act of zooming in makes an overwhelming system failure into something actionable and personally ownable.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why is the 'Shift Code' Hack described as a 'mental Ctrl+Alt+Delete'?

options.text: Because it shuts your brain down
Because it restarts your mental operating system — breaking the freeze state

questions.explanation: Like Ctrl+Alt+Delete unfreezes a hanging computer, the Shift Code ('Let me spot it and shift it') breaks problem paralysis and reboots solution-seeking mode.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What would be the correct SSI™ implication of a student who spots 5 problems and shifts all 5 in one week?

options.text: No SSI impact — it doesn't count without teacher approval
High SSI growth reflecting strong solution-seeking behavior

questions.explanation: The SSI is designed to grow with real behavior — spotting and shifting consistently is exactly what it measures and rewards.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which of these problem statements best demonstrates a complete and effective SPOT?

questions.explanation: A great SPOT is specific, observable and localised. 'Router overheats in my room' — you can see it, touch it, and act on it.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the significance of 'neural pathways' forming through repeated Spot & Shift™ practice?

options.text: They indicate that creative problem-solving becomes automatic over time

questions.explanation: Neuroscience shows repeated behaviors build stronger neural connections — meaning the more you Spot & Shift, the more naturally entrepreneurial thinking flows.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the context of Spot & Shift™, what is an 'opportunity radar'?

options.text: The trained ability to notice problems as potential starting points for solutions

questions.explanation: Entrepreneurs are described as having an 'opportunity radar' — a mental filter trained to see friction points as signals, not just annoyances.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The module says the state changes from 'Why doesn't anyone do something?' to '________'.

options.text: 'Let's see what I can do today'

questions.explanation: This shift in inner dialogue is the core mindset change — from external dependency to internal agency. That's the entrepreneurial operating system.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why does the workbook suggest doing the 'Peer Power' activity with a friend rather than alone?

options.text: Because other people can spot angles in your problem that you're too close to see
Because you need two people to fill the form

questions.explanation: Fresh eyes catch what familiarity blinds. A friend sees your problem differently — collaborative spotting is often more accurate than solo introspection.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The 'enterprising lens' in the workbook focuses on one key question. What is it?

options.text: 'Why does this always happen to me?'

questions.explanation: 'What CAN I do?' is the enterprise mindset's default question — it focuses on possibility and personal agency rather than blame or victimhood.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How does Module 1 frame the relationship between frustration and entrepreneurship?

options.text: Frustration is the starting point — the raw material that entrepreneurs convert into solutions
Entrepreneurs only work on positive ideas

questions.explanation: The module explicitly states: frustrations are 'clues to innovation' — every great business started because someone was annoyed enough to do something about it.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does 'Big Problem → Micro Problem = My Problem' teach students?

options.text: That all problems are the same size
The art of zooming in until a problem feels personally ownable and actionable
That only your own problems matter
That small problems are not worth solving

questions.explanation: Zooming in from macro to micro converts a problem from something overwhelming and external into something specific, local and personally solvable.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student's SPOT is 'My neighbourhood has no greenery.' Which of these is the most entrepreneurial SHIFT?

options.text: Write a complaint letter and wait
Organise a 'One Pot, One Spot' campaign — each friend plants one pot on their balcony

questions.explanation: The best SHIFT creates immediate, tangible, peer-led action — it's micro (one pot), owned personally, and replicable by others. Startup thinking in miniature.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does the module mean by 'entrepreneurs don't wait'?

options.text: They don't wait for permission, perfect conditions, or someone else to act first

questions.explanation: 'Entrepreneurs don't wait' is about agency — they act with what they have, where they are, even if the problem is bigger than them. The SHIFT is the beginning.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Critically evaluate: Why is specificity the most important quality of an effective SPOT?

options.text: Because specificity converts an observation into an actionable hypothesis — a prerequisite for any solution design

questions.explanation: A vague problem ('pollution is bad') has no entry point. A specific SPOT ('oil waste from 3 food stalls blocks the drain at this corner') has a geography, a cause, and a natural owner — specificity makes a problem solvable.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The Spot & Shift™ framework implicitly uses a behavioural change model. Which model does it most closely resemble?

options.text: BJ Fogg's Behaviour Model (Motivation × Ability × Trigger)

questions.explanation: BJ Fogg's model states that behaviour happens when Motivation, Ability, and a Trigger converge. SPOT creates awareness (trigger), SHIFT builds motivation, and micro-ownership ensures high ability (low effort barrier). All three align.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the systemic risk of skipping the SHIFT step and jumping directly from SPOT to Action?

options.text: You risk solving the wrong problem — acting on a symptom rather than the real, ownable micro-problem

questions.explanation: Without the SHIFT, you act on the macro-problem — wasting energy on something you can't control. The SHIFT is the targeting mechanism; without it, your action has no leverage point.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How does the Spot & Shift™ framework operationalise the concept of 'design thinking' for school students?

options.text: By compressing empathise-define-ideate into a single accessible loop: spot (empathise+define) and shift (ideate+prototype)
It doesn't relate to design thinking

questions.explanation: Design thinking's first stages — empathise (feel the frustration), define (make it specific) and ideate (shift to ownership) — are embedded invisibly in the Spot-Shift-Act sequence, making DT accessible to a 13-year-old.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Analyse the Pune student case study: What startup principle did she unknowingly apply when she gamified bottle collection?

options.text: Minimum Viable Product with a feedback loop

questions.explanation: She built the smallest possible version of her solution (badges on one group chat) that still delivered value — classic MVP thinking. The 30-participant response was her user validation, equivalent to product-market fit.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why is dopamine release specifically mentioned as part of the SHIFT's neurological effect — and not adrenaline or cortisol?

options.text: Because dopamine is tied to reward anticipation and motivation, not stress — it sustains action rather than spiking then crashing
Because cortisol is only for adults
Because adrenaline is irrelevant to the brain

questions.explanation: Cortisol = stress, adrenaline = fight-or-flight. Dopamine = motivation, reward anticipation and sustained effort. The SHIFT needs dopamine — it makes you want to continue, not just react once.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The module claims every SHIFT 'rewires your brain.' Evaluate this claim using neuroscience principles.

options.text: It is false — brains don't change
It is hyperbole with no basis
It is accurate — repeated behaviour reinforces synaptic connections (neuroplasticity), making that thought pattern more automatic over time
Only physical exercise rewires the brain

questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity is well-established. Hebb's rule ('neurons that fire together, wire together') confirms that repeatedly running the SPOT-SHIFT-ACT loop strengthens those neural circuits. The claim is scientifically valid.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: If Spot & Shift™ is Module 1 of S.U.R.G.E.™, what cognitive skill does it primarily develop, according to Bloom's Taxonomy?

options.text: Analyse (Level 4) — specifically pattern recognition in problems

questions.explanation: Spot & Shift™ primarily develops the Analyse level — students must break apart a complex situation (big problem), identify the specific mechanism (micro-problem), and recognise which piece is ownable. Higher levels come in later S.U.R.G.E.™ modules.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How does the SSI™ differ from a traditional school exam score as a learning assessment tool?

options.text: SSI™ measures real-world behavioural capability — what you DO with knowledge — not just what you can recall under pressure

questions.explanation: A school exam tests recall. SSI™ tracks applied behaviour — how many times did you spot a problem, shift your response, and take action? It's a capability credential, not a knowledge certificate.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the strategic implication of linking SSI™ data to hiring organisations through the CRISP™ protocol?

options.text: It transforms school performance into employer-relevant behavioural signals, bridging education to industry
It is only relevant for IIT students

questions.explanation: CRISP™ (Capability Readiness & Impact Signal Protocol) converts SSI™ data into hiring signals — making entrepreneurial capability visible to employers who can't read school grades for it. This is the macro system designed into YoungPreneurs.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: A student argues: 'I can't shift my problem because I don't have resources or authority.' Evaluate this objection using Spot & Shift™ logic.

options.text: The student is correct — resources are the first requirement
The student is misidentifying the barrier — Spot & Shift asks for the smallest ownable piece, which rarely requires resources or authority
They should wait until they are older
The framework does not address this

questions.explanation: Resource scarcity is often assumed, not real. The framework's genius is in 'micro-ownership' — the first action is almost always low or zero-resource. The Pune student needed no budget, just will and a WhatsApp group.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Compare 'internal locus of control' (built by Spot & Shift™) with 'external locus of control' and explain why the former is linked to entrepreneurial success.

options.text: External locus is better for business
Internal locus = belief that your actions determine outcomes; external = outcomes are controlled by luck or others. Entrepreneurs need internal locus to persist through uncertainty
Locus of control is irrelevant to business

questions.explanation: Research (Rotter, 1954; and decades since) shows people with internal locus of control are more likely to take initiative, persist despite failure, and create new ventures. Spot & Shift™ builds this trait from Class 8 onward.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why does the module use the word 'own' rather than 'solve' in the SHIFT prompt ('Name one small part you could possibly OWN')?

options.text: Because 'solve' implies completion — 'own' implies ongoing commitment and personal stewardship, which is more entrepreneurially accurate
Because 'solve' is too difficult for students
Because the two words mean the same thing

questions.explanation: 'Solve' sets up a pass-fail binary and implies the problem disappears. 'Own' is ongoing — you claim the problem as yours to steward. This is the entrepreneur's actual relationship with challenges.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The module asks students to 'post' their action in a Mindset Journal. What pedagogical principle does this reflect?

options.text: Performative learning — making thinking visible creates accountability and deepens reflection

questions.explanation: Externalising thinking (journalling, posting, sharing) is a proven metacognitive technique. It forces students to articulate their reasoning, making learning more durable and creating peer accountability loops.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Evaluate: Is the '24-hour' timeframe for taking a first action arbitrary, or does it serve a specific psychological purpose?

options.text: Deliberate — 24 hours prevents the intention-action gap from widening; ideas have a short half-life and immediate action builds habit strength
It is borrowed from military protocols

questions.explanation: The intention-action gap is real and well-documented. The longer between insight and action, the less likely action happens. 24 hours creates urgency without panic — and the first action, however small, is what builds the habit loop.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How would you design a 'Spot & Shift™ Sprint' for a Class 12 student preparing for entrepreneurship beyond school?

options.text: Focus only on global problems like climate change
Apply the same framework but increase the scope — from micro-action to a testable prototype within 7 days, with real stakeholder feedback
Skip the SPOT and go straight to pitching
Only do it in a classroom setting

questions.explanation: For Class 12, the scope scales: SPOT (industry-level frustration) → SHIFT (specific user segment + pain point) → ACTION (prototype/MVP in a week, tested with 5 real people). The framework is the same; the ambition level escalates.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does the 'IDEA DNA' metaphor achieve pedagogically that a simpler term like 'learning' would not?

options.text: It creates identity ownership — students see entrepreneurial capability as part of who they ARE, not just something they studied

questions.explanation: Framing entrepreneurial thinking as 'DNA' encodes it as intrinsic identity, not external knowledge. Students don't say 'I learned about spotting problems' — they say 'My S nucleotide is activated.' Identity-based learning produces far more durable behaviour change.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why might ZUNNOVA™ use a Socratic (questioning) approach rather than a direct-answer approach for Class 11–12 students?

options.text: Because the Socratic method forces higher-order thinking — students must arrive at insight themselves, creating deeper cognitive ownership
Because AI can't give direct answers

questions.explanation: Research on productive failure and Socratic dialogue shows that self-generated insights are retained far longer than provided answers. ZUNNOVA™ asking 'What's the smallest piece you could own?' is more powerful than telling you the answer.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Analyse the power dynamics implicit in the statement 'I'm too young' — and explain how Spot & Shift™ subverts them.

options.text: It agrees — young people should wait
'I'm too young' is an externally imposed constraint accepted as internal truth; Spot & Shift™ replaces systemic permission-seeking with personal micro-action, bypassing gatekeepers
Age is irrelevant to the framework

questions.explanation: The most revolutionary thing Spot & Shift™ does is make permission unnecessary. You don't need a title, an office or adult approval to own the plastic bottles at your bus stop. Micro-ownership is permission-free. This is profoundly anti-hierarchical.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: If a student consistently produces high-quality SPOTs but fails to SHIFT, what does this reveal about their entrepreneurial development stage?

options.text: They are ready to launch a company
They have strong empathy and observation skills but lack agency activation — they are stuck between awareness and ownership
They are performing at the highest level

questions.explanation: Spotting without shifting is empathy without agency — common in design researchers and journalists, not yet in entrepreneurs. The SHIFT is where the entrepreneurial identity activates. This student needs interventions around personal ownership and risk tolerance.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: The Future Titans™ challenge is described as a national innovation competition. How does it serve as a 'GTM activation mechanism' for YoungPreneurs?

options.text: It is only for marketing purposes
It creates a publicly visible, competitive arena that demonstrates student capability at scale — creating demand from schools, parents, and industry simultaneously

questions.explanation: Future Titans™ is the flywheel: students want to compete → schools want the credibility → industry wants the talent pipeline → media wants the story. The competition is the demand engine that pulls all stakeholders toward the platform.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Critically assess: Can the Spot & Shift™ framework produce false positives — where students believe they are shifting when they are actually just reframing complaints more cleverly?

options.text: No, because the framework is perfect
Yes — without a concrete, time-bound action step, a 'shift' can remain purely cognitive — the ACTION element is what distinguishes real from performative shifting

questions.explanation: The weakest version of Spot & Shift™ is when the SHIFT is intellectual but the ACTION is absent. 'I'll think about owning this problem' is not a shift — it's a sophisticated complaint. The framework needs the 24-hour action anchor to prevent this failure mode.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How does the 'Certified Spotter' badge function as a motivational instrument beyond simple gamification?

options.text: It creates the first artefact of entrepreneurial identity — a credential that signals to the student and others that they have taken a specific capability step, anchoring future behaviour

questions.explanation: Identity credentials shape behaviour. A student who now calls themselves a 'Certified Spotter' has an identity to live up to. This is identity-based habit formation — proven to be more durable than reward-based motivation alone.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In what way does the 'Peer Power' activity scale the Spot & Shift™ framework beyond individual cognition?

options.text: It doesn't — peer activities are just for fun
It introduces distributed problem-sensing — each peer brings different lived contexts, collectively generating more diverse and precise SPOTs than any individual could alone

questions.explanation: Distributed sensing is a systems design principle — multiple observers catch more signals than one. Peer Power applies this to entrepreneurial problem-spotting, creating a proto-team dynamic even at the individual learning stage.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the philosophical argument embedded in the tagline 'Complaints are just solutions in disguise'?

options.text: It implies we should never express frustration
It posits that every frustration contains an implicit desired state — and that desired state is the blueprint of the solution waiting to be built
It suggests all complaints are trivial
It is a marketing slogan with no deeper meaning

questions.explanation: Every complaint contains an embedded aspiration: 'WiFi sucks' means 'I want reliable connectivity.' The negative (complaint) and the positive (desired state) are two faces of the same insight. The entrepreneur flips the coin and builds toward the positive.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Analyse how the S.U.R.G.E.™ framework's five modules might be designed to progressively develop entrepreneurial thinking from observation to execution.

options.text: SPOT (awareness) → UNBUNDLE (deconstruct) → REFRAME (reposition) → GENERATE (create options) → EXECUTE (build and test) — a compressed entrepreneurial process from problem to prototype
They repeat the same skill in different ways

questions.explanation: S.U.R.G.E.™ is a sequenced scaffold: Module 1 (Spot) builds observation, Module 2 (Unbundle) builds analysis, Module 3 (Reframe) builds creative positioning, Module 4 (Generate) builds ideation, Module 5 (Execute) builds prototyping. Together they compress the full entrepreneurial design cycle into a school curriculum.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: From an investor's perspective, why is a student's SSI™ score a more investable signal than their school exam rank?

options.text: Because SSI™ tracks real behavioural iterations — the frequency and quality of problem-spotting and shifting — which predicts entrepreneurial output better than subject knowledge

questions.explanation: An investor bets on behaviour under uncertainty. Exam scores predict performance in structured environments. SSI™ predicts what someone does when confronted with unstructured, real-world friction — which is exactly what startup life requires.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How does the module's reference to 'opportunity radar' reflect the concept of 'prepared mind' in innovation theory?

options.text: It is unrelated to innovation theory
Pasteur's principle — 'Chance favours the prepared mind' — suggests that innovation opportunity is only visible to those already tuned to its signal; the 'opportunity radar' is that preparation
It refers to a scanning technology

questions.explanation: Louis Pasteur's famous maxim underpins this: the same environment looks like a problem-graveyard to one person and an opportunity landscape to another. Spot & Shift™ literally trains the prepared mind — so when opportunity appears, you're already scanning for it.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: If a student uses Spot & Shift™ to identify a problem that is socially sensitive (e.g., caste discrimination at school), what additional responsibility does the framework create for educators?

options.text: Ignore it — the framework isn't for social issues

The framework creates a duty of care: educators must guide students to shift with sensitivity, safety, and appropriate scale — not every SPOT requires individual action; some require systemic escalation
Discourage students from spotting social problems

questions.explanation: When a SPOT reveals a systemic injustice, the 'micro-ownership' principle must be balanced against scale, safety and power dynamics. Great educators using this framework will distinguish between problems a student can own and problems that require adult, institutional or community-level response.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Synthesise: How does Module 1 of S.U.R.G.E.™ plant the foundational belief required for all entrepreneurship — and why is placing it first strategically correct?

options.text: It teaches finance, which is the foundation
It establishes personal agency — the belief that 'I can own a piece of this' — without which no amount of ideation, networking, or funding produces an entrepreneur
It is first simply by convention

questions.explanation: Before tools, techniques or tactics, an entrepreneur needs one belief: 'I am someone who acts on problems.' Module 1's singular job is to install that belief — once. If a student leaves Module 1 knowing they can own even one piece of one problem, the entire S.U.R.G.E.™ system can build on that. Agency is the soil; everything else is the crop.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the bus stop example, what was the visible problem?

questions.subject: entrepreneurship

questions.explanation: The 5 Whys technique helps you drill down past symptoms to find the root cause of a problem.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Who are "Helpers" in your stakeholder map?

questions.question: What does the star symbol mean in the Stakeholder Map?

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is "Dragon Ball Data"?

options.text: Real-world data to power up your idea

questions.explanation: Dragon Ball Data refers to real-world data that powers up your idea, just like Dragon Balls power up characters.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How many questions are in the Micro-Survey?
questions.explanation: The Micro-Survey contains exactly 3 focused questions designed to gather quick insights from people.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the final output of Module 2?
questions.explanation: The Insight Card is the final deliverable of Module 2, summarizing your root cause, key data, and next move.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In Module 1, what did you claim ownership of?
questions.explanation: In Module 1 (Spot & Shift), students claimed ownership of a micro-problem — a small, actionable piece of a bigger issue.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does "Unbundle" mean in this module?

options.text: To break a big problem into small pieces

questions.explanation: Unbundle means to break a big, tangled problem into smaller, understandable pieces that you can work with.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which of these is a "Constraint"?
questions.explanation: Constraints are limitations like time, money, or rules that restrict what solutions are possible.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Who are "Deciders"?
questions.explanation: Deciders are people who have authority to make rules, approve changes, or allocate resources related to the problem.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What should you count during a Field Check?

options.text: Number of bottles, wrappers, or relevant items
Number of clouds in the sky

questions.explanation: During a Field Check, you count items directly related to your problem — like bottles, wrappers, or other observable evidence.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does "Understand" help you turn your idea into?
questions.explanation: The Understand phase transforms your idea from a vague feeling into a fact-based mission backed by real data and root cause analysis.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the bus stop example, what was one root cause?
questions.explanation: One root cause discovered through the 5 Whys was that there was no bin available at the bus stop.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the "Annoying Little Sibling Method" another name for?
questions.explanation: The 5 Whys is humorously called the 'Annoying Little Sibling Method' because it involves repeatedly asking 'Why?' like a persistent younger sibling.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What kind of people are in the "Top Box" of the Stakeholder Map?
questions.explanation: The Top Box of the Stakeholder Map contains the Affected — people who directly experience the problem.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What kind of people are in the "Right Box" of the Stakeholder Map?
questions.explanation: The Right Box contains Helpers — people who have the ability and willingness to assist in solving the problem.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the first question in the 3-question micro-survey?

options.text: Do you notice the bottles here?

questions.explanation: The first micro-survey question checks awareness by asking if people notice the problem (e.g., bottles).

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the second question in the micro-survey about?
questions.explanation: The second question explores people's current habits related to the problem, such as what they do with a bottle.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the third question in the micro-survey about?
questions.explanation: The third question gauges willingness to participate in a potential solution, like joining a bottle collection game.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does "peak time" mean in data collection?

options.text: The time when most waste appears

questions.explanation: Peak time refers to when the problem is most visible or intense, such as when the most waste appears.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What should you do after collecting your data?
questions.explanation: After collecting data through your Field Check and micro-survey, you compile everything into an Insight Card.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the Insight Card, what goes under "Key Number"?

options.text: A data point from your Field Check

questions.explanation: The Key Number is a specific, measurable data point from your Field Check that quantifies the problem.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the bus stop example, what was the "Surprising Insight"?

options.text: People might join if it's a game

questions.explanation: The surprising insight was that people expressed willingness to participate if the solution was gamified.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the "Next Move" on the Insight Card?
questions.explanation: The Next Move is a concrete, small-scale action — typically proposing a small pilot to test your solution idea.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does Module 3 focus on?
questions.explanation: Module 3 is 'Reframe & Run,' which follows Module 2 and focuses on reframing the problem and running a pilot.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is a "Micro-Problem"?

options.text: A tiny, ownable piece of a bigger problem

questions.explanation: A micro-problem is a small, specific, ownable piece of a larger problem that one person or team can tackle.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why do we talk to "Helpers" first?

options.text: They are easiest to reach and most likely to help

questions.explanation: Helpers are prioritized because they are the most accessible and willing to assist, making them the best starting point.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What does "Dragon Ball" refer to in "Dragon Ball Data"?

options.text: Energy to power up your idea

questions.explanation: Like Dragon Balls that give energy and power, Dragon Ball Data gives your idea the power of real evidence.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: How many people should you ask for the micro-survey?
questions.explanation: The micro-survey is designed to be quick — asking 3 to 5 people gives you useful directional data without requiring a large sample.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: What is the purpose of the Stakeholder Map?

options.text: To understand who is connected to the problem

questions.explanation: The Stakeholder Map helps you identify and understand all the people connected to your problem and their roles.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which of these is an example of a "Constraint"?
questions.explanation: School rules are a constraint because they limit what actions or solutions are possible within that environment.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: You see broken glass in the park. Using the 5 Whys, you find the root cause is "no safe disposal for broken glass." What is the first Why likely to be?
questions.explanation: The first Why addresses the immediate visible problem — why glass is breaking — before drilling deeper into disposal issues.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: You map stakeholders for "cafeteria food waste." Who is a Decider?
questions.explanation: The cafeteria manager is the Decider because they have authority over food operations and can approve changes.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: During a Field Check, you notice most waste appears right after lunch. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Noticing that waste peaks after lunch is identifying a pattern — a recurring observation that helps focus your solution.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Your micro-survey shows 4/5 people would join a "clean-up game." What does this tell you?
questions.explanation: A strong majority expressing interest in a game suggests that gamification could be an effective approach to your solution.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which stakeholder is most likely to have a star for a "no library books returned" problem?
questions.explanation: The librarian is the most accessible and relevant person you can talk to within 24 hours about unreturned books.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: You ask "Why wasn't the bin replaced?" That is the _____ Why in the 5 Whys sequence.
questions.explanation: Asking why the bin wasn't replaced is a follow-up question that typically comes as the second or third Why in the sequence.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Your Insight Card says "Root Cause: No easy reporting system." What is a good Next Move?
questions.explanation: If the root cause is no reporting system, a logical next move is to design a simple reporting mechanism like a card or form.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Why is the "10-Minute Field Check" better than guessing?
questions.explanation: The Field Check provides real, observable data from the actual environment, which is far more reliable than assumptions or guesses.

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: In the bus stop example, the "Key Number" was 37. What does it represent?

questions.subject: entrepreneurship
questions.question: Which of these is NOT a stakeholder in "water spilled near the fountain"?
